results.title: السبت .. التعاون والفتح يبحثان عن الفوز الأول
results.description:
يضع التعاون وضيفه الفتح، النقاط الثلاث هدفاً رئيساً لهما، عندما يلتقيان، اليوم السبت على ملعب نادي التعاون ببريدة، برسم منافسات الجولة الخامسة لدوري روشن السعودي.

ويتفوق التعاون على ضيفه بفارق انتصار، في دوري المحترفين، حيث التقيا في دوري المحترفين 32 مرة، فاز التعاون في 12 مباراة، وفاز الفتح في 11 مباراة، وحضر التعادل في 9 مباريات، سجل خلالها هجوم التعاون 45 هدفاً، بينما سجل هجوم الفتح 39 هدفًا.

ويدخل الفريقان المباراة بظروف متشابهة على مستوى النتائج، فكل منهما تعادل في مباراتين وخسر مثلها ولم يحققا أي فوز.

وفاجأ التعاون الجميع بنتائجه الغير منتظرة، فعلى الرغم من تكامل صفوفه، إلا أنه لم يحقق أي حالة فوز، ويطمح هذا المساء إلى استعادة توازنه وتسجيل فوزه الأول.

ويمتلك التعاون أسماء مميزة، على غرار الهداف المغربي عبدالرزاق حمدالله ومواطنه أشرف المهديوي والجزائري زين الدين بالعيد والألباني نديم بايرامي والبرازيلي مايلسون والبلغاري مارين بيتكوف والليبيري أوسكار دورلي.

ولا يختلف الفتح كثيراً عن مضيفه، فالفريق رغم الصفقات الأجنبية والمحلية التي أبرمها إلا أنه لم ينتصر في أي مباراة، ويأمل هذا المساء، في تجاوز أزمة النتائج السابقة والعودة بالعلامة الكاملة.

ويبرز في صفوف الفتح، المغربي مراد باتنا ومواطنه مروان سعدان والقمري زايدو يوسف والسلوفاكي لوكاس هراسلين والتوغولي كينيدي بواتينغ والعاجي ويلفريد كانجا .

results.title: Saudi LEAP 2026 ends with nearly $15 billion in deals, investments
results.description: Saudi LEAP 2026 ends with nearly $15 billion in deals, investments The four-day conference brought together global technology and investment companies at a time when Riyadh is accelerating its push into the digital economy. Friday 04/09/2026 Visitors make their way to the main hall during the opening ceremony of the technology event LEAP in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, August 31, 2026. RIYADH Saudi Arabia’s LEAP 2026 technology conference ended in Riyadh with announcements, investments and agreements worth nearly $15 billion, underscoring the kingdom’s growing focus on artificial intelligence, digital technologies and space as it seeks to reshape its economy. The four-day conference, organised by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, the Saudi Federation for Cybersecurity, Programming and Drones, Tahaluf and the Events Investment Fund under the theme “Into New Worlds”, brought together global technology and investment companies at a time when Riyadh is accelerating its push into the digital economy. The value of the announcements goes beyond the commercial tally of a technology conference. It reflects a broader Saudi strategy to attract investment into sectors seen as potential engines of global growth in the coming years, particularly AI infrastructure, data centres, cloud computing, advanced computing and technology manufacturing. Saudi Arabia is increasingly treating technology not as another sector to add to the economy, but as a means of reshaping the economy itself, reducing its dependence on oil revenues and creating new sources of growth and investment. Artificial intelligence was at the centre of LEAP, reflecting the priority Riyadh has given the sector under its economic diversification strategy. The kingdom is seeking to compete not only by attracting technology companies, but by building the infrastructure needed to develop and deploy AI, from data centres and cloud computing to energy, telecommunications and human capital. The investments announced at LEAP are part of that wider technology ecosystem rather than simply purchases of digital products or services. Amazon Web Services said its first cloud infrastructure region in Saudi Arabia would launch in December 2026 as part of a planned investment of more than $5.3 billion. AWS also expanded its partnership with HUMAIN, a Saudi AI company owned by the Public Investment Fund, to provide up to 50 megawatts of capacity within the kingdom’s first AI zone by 2028. The partnership will make HUMAIN’s Arabic-language ALLAM model available through Amazon Bedrock and HUMAIN Fabric through AWS Marketplace, supporting advanced computing and the development and operation of AI applications. Al Moammar Information Systems announced a $1.2 billion investment to expand its data centres and increase capacity to 192 megawatts, while NHC Innovation announced an $800 million investment to develop Khuzam Digital Valley, with capacity that can be expanded to 65 megawatts by 2033. Adobe announced a commitment worth more than $4 billion as part of an expanded partnership with the Saudi Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and HUMAIN. By the end of 2026, the partnership is expected to provide more than 27 million eligible citizens and residents aged 13 and above with free access to Adobe Firefly Standard and Adobe Express Premium features for 12 months. The partnership also includes development of an image-generation model using Adobe Firefly Foundry with HUMAIN, designed to reflect Saudi culture and local context and support the creation of Arabic-language content. HUMAIN announced a series of other partnerships aimed at building an integrated domestic AI ecosystem spanning computing power, infrastructure and applications. It is working with Together AI to provide 55 megawatts of dedicated AI capacity and develop a 250-megawatt data centre, while a partnership with AMD envisages an initial 25 megawatts and an infrastructure target of 250 megawatts over the next two to three years. In NEOM’s Oxagon, HUMAIN and DataVolt have begun construction of a 100-megawatt initial phase of an AI data centre. HUMAIN also launched an AI cloud in Saudi Arabia powered by NVIDIA HGX B300 Blackwell Ultra systems. The platform currently provides 1.1 megawatts of operational AI infrastructure and has recorded utilisation of more than 90%, with plans to expand capacity to 35.1 megawatts by 2027. The technology push is part of an effort to build Saudi Arabia’s position in a market dominated by competition among the United States, China, Europe and Asian and Gulf economies. Riyadh is seeking to use its financial resources, large domestic market and substantial government investment to attract global companies and build a technology ecosystem within the kingdom. The strategy forms a central part of Saudi Arabia’s broader economic transformation under Vision 2030. Rather than treating the eventual decline in oil’s importance as a problem that must simply be managed, the kingdom is seeking to use the revenues and financial capacity generated by oil to finance the transition into new sectors. Under that model, oil helps finance the transformation, while the transformation is intended to create a more diversified economy less exposed to fluctuations in energy prices. The strategy has gained importance as data, computing, AI and the energy required to operate data centres have become increasingly linked to economic security as well as technological development. One of the objectives of hosting a conference of LEAP’s scale is to move Saudi Arabia from being primarily a consumer of technology to becoming a regional centre for developing and localising it. That requires attracting global companies, developing domestic businesses, training skilled workers, expanding digital infrastructure and linking public and private investment. Saudi Arabia has several advantages in pursuing that goal, including its investment capacity, the Public Investment Fund, the government’s ability to execute large-scale projects and its geographical position between Asian, European and African markets. The scale of investment alone, however, will not guarantee the creation of technology companies capable of competing globally. Education, scientific research, specialised talent, regulation and the ability of start-ups to scale will be critical to the next phase. The kingdom’s technology transformation also has implications beyond the economy. Countries able to attract technology companies, capital and talent can increasingly become new centres of influence. LEAP’s investments can be viewed as part of Riyadh’s effort to strengthen its position as a regional economic hub not only in energy and finance, but also in technology. AI requires energy, data centres require substantial infrastructure, and technology companies require capital and markets. Saudi Arabia has many of these ingredients and is seeking to bring them together within a single ecosystem. That gives technology investment a strategic dimension at a time when global competition is increasingly focused on new value chains linked to chips, computing, data and artificial intelligence. Saudi Arabia is not alone in pursuing that strategy. The United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other Gulf states are also investing heavily in AI, data centres and advanced technologies. The size of the Saudi market and Riyadh’s investment capacity, however, give its approach a different scale. The kingdom is seeking to combine a large domestic market, government investment, global companies and major development projects to create a technology ecosystem extending beyond the technology sector itself. LEAP’s final announcements included more than $2.5 billion in investments on its second day and another $857 million in technology and manufacturing investments on its third day, spanning cloud infrastructure, data centre manufacturing and venture funding. The conference also saw nearly $293 million in venture activity announced across 11 deals on its third day, including nine funding rounds worth $126.15 million involving companies in AI, fintech, travel, gaming, human resources and automotive services. Ula Capital partnered with South Korea’s FuturePlay to launch a $100 million fund aimed at connecting deep-tech investment opportunities between Saudi Arabia and South Korea. Saudi authorities also placed emphasis on developing the workforce needed to support the technology expansion. The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Saudi Digital Academy launched a Gemini initiative with Google to provide 1 million Saudi university students with access to advanced AI tools. An AI academy developed with WeCloudData will train educators, university faculty, start-up founders and tens of thousands of online learners. AWS said its Amazon Academy, launched with the ministry, aims to train more than 100,000 Saudis in cloud, AI, logistics and retail, while its Saudi Arabia Women’s Skills Initiative is working with 11 higher education institutions and training up to 10,000 women. The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority is also working to measure and improve institutional readiness through the National AI Index. The test for Saudi Arabia will be whether the commitments announced at LEAP can be converted into operating projects, high-quality jobs, globally competitive local companies, patents and technology products capable of being exported abroad. LEAP’s sixth edition is scheduled to take place in Riyadh from April 12 to 15, 2027.
